scenes.visual: Show the title: From Food to Usable Nutrients. Preview a meal, small molecules and the gut lining.

scenes.tts: An animal can use a meal only after food is broken into molecules small enough to cross the gut lining. The gut breaks food down, absorbs nutrients, water and salts, and eliminates what is left. Different regions do different jobs. In humans, most digestion and nutrient absorption happen in the small intestine. Its folds, villi and microvilli multiply the surface where nutrients cross into the body.

scenes.visual: Follow food along a simplified human gut. Show large food molecules becoming small subunits, then crossing the small-intestinal lining. Distinguish material moving along the tube from nutrients crossing its wall. Zoom from folds to villi to microvilli; label the small intestine as the main site of digestion and nutrient absorption.

scenes.tts: Teeth grind food. The stomach mixes it with acid and enzymes. The pancreas sends digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the small intestine. Bicarbonate neutralizes acid. Bile salts break fat drops into smaller droplets that lipase can reach. Enzymes split molecules; bile is not an enzyme. Most absorbed sugars and amino acids enter blood. Most absorbed fat leaves through lymph vessels. The large intestine absorbs water and salts.

scenes.visual: Trace teeth, stomach and small intestine in sequence. Add pancreatic enzyme and bicarbonate arrows, then bile from liver through gallbladder. Compare enzymes splitting molecules with bile dispersing fat droplets. At a villus, send sugars and amino acids to a blood capillary and fat particles to a lacteal labelled lymph vessel. End on water and salt absorption in the large intestine.

scenes.tts: Gut designs differ with diet and ancestry. A cow ferments food before its acid-secreting stomach region. A horse ferments after the small intestine. Gut length alone is no simple guide to diet.

scenes.visual: Compare simplified cow and horse gut maps. Mark fermentation before the cow's acid-secreting region and after the horse's small intestine, without implying that a cow has separate stomachs. Show diet, body size and ancestry beside a gut-length ruler; avoid a universal long-herbivore, short-carnivore rule.

scenes.tts: Who breaks down the fiber? Microbes ferment cellulose and release short-chain fatty acids, which the host absorbs. Cows digest microbes that pass into the acid-secreting stomach compartment. Horses ferment in the cecum and colon. Rabbits ferment in the cecum too. They eat soft cecal pellets, sending microbes and their protein through the stomach and small intestine for digestion and absorption.

scenes.visual: Place microbes in the cow's rumen and reticulum and the horse's cecum and colon. Show cellulose becoming short-chain fatty acids and crossing into the host. Follow cow microbes downstream into the acid-secreting abomasum for digestion. Add a rabbit panel with a soft-cecal-pellet loop back to the mouth, then through stomach and small intestine to recover microbial protein.

scenes.tts: Nerves and hormones coordinate the work. Gut-wall nerves run local reflexes. In Pavlov's dogs, eating triggered stomach juice even when food never reached the stomach. Cutting both vagus nerves stopped that response. This showed nervous control before food arrived.

scenes.visual: First show local nerve circuits in the gut wall controlling peristalsis. Then briefly reuse the sham-feeding dog: swallowed food exits the opened esophagus, while acid juice drains through the gastric fistula after a delay. Cross both vagus lines and stop the eating-triggered secretion. Label the result as evidence in dogs; do not imply that cutting the vagus abolishes every phase of secretion.

scenes.tts: Hormones travel in blood. Food in the stomach brings out gastrin, which increases acid secretion.
scenes.narration: Hormones travel in blood. Food in the stomach brings out gastrin, which increases acid secretion.
scenes.caption: Hormones travel in blood. Food in the stomach brings out gastrin, which increases acid secretion.
scenes.visual: Reuse stomach G cells and the blood bar. Food triggers gastrin release into blood; returning hormone signals increase stomach acid.

scenes.tts: Acid entering the duodenum brings out secretin, which drives pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. Fats and proteins bring out C C K, which drives pancreatic enzyme release and gallbladder contraction to release bile.
scenes.narration: Acid entering the duodenum brings out secretin, which drives pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. Fats and proteins bring out CCK, which drives pancreatic enzyme release and gallbladder contraction to release bile.
scenes.caption: Acid entering the duodenum brings out secretin, which drives pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. Fats and proteins bring out CCK, which drives pancreatic enzyme release and gallbladder contraction to release bile.
scenes.visual: Reuse the duodenum, pancreas, gallbladder and blood bar. Show acid triggering secretin, then pancreatic bicarbonate neutralizing acid. Show fats and proteins triggering CCK, then pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder bile entering the duodenum. Keep hormone travel through blood visually distinct from secretion into the gut.

scenes.tts: Finally, an essential nutrient must come from food because an animal cannot make enough. Requirements differ. Humans need dietary vitamin C. Cats need dietary taurine, which adult humans make.

scenes.visual: Show a food-to-animal arrow labelled essential when the animal cannot make enough of a nutrient. Compare human dietary vitamin C with cat dietary taurine; show adult humans making taurine. End on absorbed nutrients entering the body.
